newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says military advance mission in Tirana.
newsitem.headline: Italy says military advance mission in Tirana.

text.p: Italy on Tuesday said military experts from six countries had flown to Albania for talks on the possible deployment of a multinational protection force as part of a planned European Union relief mission.

Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta said the team comprised representatives of the four countries that make up the Florence-based Eurofor force -- conceived by France, Italy, Portugal and Spain for peacekeeping and relief operations -- as well as a Greek and an Austrian, both generals.
"The Albanian government re-iterated its desire to have a multinational force in Albania," Andreatta said after talks with Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.
"We are waiting for certain European countries which have expressed a readiness to contribute troops to do so in order to allow the multinational force to get going," he said.

EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday again shied away from backing full-scale military intervention in Albania, where large areas of the south are in the hands of armed rebels and lawless mafias.

But they welcomed the efforts of certain EU states to assemble a force "under the appropriate international aegis" to provide security for the delivery of food and medical relief as part of an EU mission to the impoverished Balkan state.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, speaking after EU foreign ministers met Fino in Rome on Tuesday, said he expected a decision on the size of the force to be taken within days.
"Its dimensions will depend on the objectives which it is set," Dini said, adding that Italy would not intervene on its own in the chaos-hit Balkan state.

Non-EU members Turkey and Romania have said they are willing to join such a force and Greek deputy foreign minister George Papandreou, who also met Fini separately in Rome, said Athens was likewise prepared to contribute.
"We would be willing to offer either police or troops," Papandreou told Reuters. "We'd be under the command of the multinational force...so they would have the say as to where we would go," he said.

The need for some sort of outside armed force to protect aid convoys from gunmen who rule parts of the country after looting thousands of weapons from army depots was graphically underlined by an Italian helicopter evacuation on Tuesday of four doctors.

The doctors, members of an Italian Red Cross relief mission in the southern rebel-held city of Vlore, were flown out with a wounded gunman whose comrades had taken them hostage demanding that he be flown to Italy for medical treatment.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the EU presidency, said an advisory team -- the second in as many weeks -- would leave for Albania on Wednesday to assess the scale of the planned relief mission.
The 54-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is regarded by countries ready to commit forces to the mission as the appropriate forum to give the go-ahead.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said adequate security for an EU relief mission need not be large and highlighted the distaste for intervention.
"To send an army to Albania would risk becoming involved in the internal affairs of what is a very unstable country. That would be unwise and does not seem to be necessary," he said.
